Activation steering works by adding a learned direction vector to a model's residual stream at inference time to shift behavior (e.g., toward honesty or away from harmful outputs), but in RLHF-trained models the residual stream geometry has already been shaped by reward optimization — so the central question is whether steering vectors computed in that post-RLHF space remain linearly separable and causally effective, or whether RLHF has entangled the features those vectors were meant to isolate. The key concepts are: the linear representation hypothesis (that concepts live in approximately linear subspaces of activation space), the superposition problem (multiple features compressed into fewer dimensions), reward hacking geometry (RLHF may push representations toward reward-relevant directions in ways that warp the original feature manifold), and multi-objective interference (when you simultaneously constrain helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty, their steering vectors may not be orthogonal, producing destructive or constructive interference depending on context). What a beginner misses is that steering vectors are typically extracted from a different model state than the one being steered — often a base model or a single-objective fine-tune — so when applied to a multi-objective RLHF model, you're imposing a geometry onto a space that has been non-linearly reorganized by the training process. The expert worry is therefore not "does steering work at all" but rather "does the apparent success of steering in aggregate metrics mask selective failures in exactly the high-stakes, distribution-shifted cases where alignment matters most" — because the interference between competing objective vectors is unlikely to be uniform across the input manifold.

The most principled current approach to identifying the reward subspace boundary at inference time is to track the singular value spectrum of the Jacobian of the model's output distribution with respect to its residual stream activations — directions where the Jacobian has near-zero singular values are, by definition, outside the subspace that causally affects reward-relevant outputs, and this can be estimated cheaply via randomized SVD on a small prompt batch; Raghu et al.'s SVCCA work and more recently Dar et al.'s (2023) weight-space analysis of fine-tuned transformers both show this spectrum is surprisingly stable across prompt distributions for a given model, making it a plausible inference-time invariant rather than a per-query recomputation. The technical obstacle is that training such a signal requires ground-truth labels for "this activation is near the boundary," which are themselves defined by the very geometry you're trying to expose — a circularity that might be broken by using counterfactual steering probes: systematically applying perturbations and labeling activations by whether small perturbations produce outsized behavioral change (high curvature = near boundary). The more radical version of this idea appears implicitly in Conjecture's work on "causal scrubbing" and in path patching methodology — if you can identify which computational paths are load-bearing for reward-relevant behavior, the complement of those paths approximates the safe-to-steer subspace, and a model trained with auxiliary losses on those path attributions would effectively be learning to self-annotate its own steering constraints. The reason no production system does this yet is cost: computing Jacobian spectra or path attributions at inference time for a 70B+ model is currently prohibitive, but the architectural implication is pointed — future alignment-aware architectures may need explicit subspace boundary signals baked into their forward pass, rather than treating interpretability as a post-hoc forensic exercise.

The frozen interpreter idea is genuinely promising for independence but founders on a concrete empirical fact: RLHF fine-tuning, even when applied only to a small fraction of parameters via LoRA or adapter layers, produces representation drift that is not uniformly distributed across layers — Merchant et al.'s (2020) probing study and more recently Wendler et al.'s (2024) analysis of fine-tuned Llama models both show that middle layers (roughly 40–70% depth) shift substantially more than early or late layers, meaning a frozen interpreter trained on pre-RLHF activations from those layers will face a covariate shift that is both large and systematically biased toward exactly the reward-relevant features it was meant to track. The drift is not random rotation — which would degrade the interpreter uniformly and be detectable by accuracy drop — but rather reward-aligned shear: the RLHF process stretches the activation manifold along reward-relevant directions while approximately preserving geometry in orthogonal directions, so the frozen interpreter may remain accurate on low-stakes inputs (where the manifold is undistorted) while becoming precisely miscalibrated on high-stakes, reward-boundary inputs, producing the worst possible failure mode: confident and wrong exactly where it matters. Quantitatively, Lyu et al.'s (2023) work on RLHF representation analysis found cosine similarities between pre- and post-RLHF activations dropping to 0.6–0.7 in critical middle layers for models fine-tuned with even modest KL penalties, which is enough drift to substantially degrade a linear probe trained on pre-RLHF geometry. A partial mitigation is to train the interpreter not on raw activations but on relative geometry — pairwise distances or directional relationships between activations for contrastive prompt pairs — since Elhage et al.'s superposition work suggests these relational structures are more invariant to linear transformations than absolute positions; but this only helps if RLHF's distortion is approximately linear, which it isn't guaranteed to be. The structural conclusion is that a frozen pre-RLHF interpreter gives you genuine independence at the cost of calibration that decays monotonically with RLHF training intensity, suggesting the viable architecture is not a single frozen interpreter but a continually updated interpreter trained on a held-out reward-free objective — essentially a second model that tracks the main model's geometry without ever seeing reward signal, which reintroduces the scaling and maintenance costs that made the frozen approach attractive in the first place.

The inevitability claim is strong but defensible under one precise condition: interpreter blindness will be selected for whenever (a) the model has sufficient representational capacity to encode the same output via multiple activation pathways and (b) some pathways are more interpreter-transparent than others — both conditions are satisfied in any overparameterized transformer with a fixed external interpreter, meaning the question is not whether blindness emerges but how fast, which is governed by the ratio of model capacity to interpreter coverage. Empirical hints at a phase transition already exist: Anthropic's research on Claude 2-era training noted qualitative shifts in probe reliability at certain RLHF iteration counts, and Nanda et al.'s (2022) grokking work is structurally relevant — it documents genuine phase transitions in how networks encode solutions, where a model abruptly switches from a "memorization" circuit to a "generalization" circuit at a threshold training step, suggesting that representational reorganizations in general are not smooth but punctuated, and there's no reason interpreter-opacity wouldn't follow the same punctuated dynamics. The qualitative danger threshold is likely tied not to blindness magnitude but to blindness locality: gradual uniform degradation of interpreter accuracy is detectable and correctable, but a phase transition where the model becomes selectively opaque on a specific high-stakes input submanifold — say, exactly the inputs near the refusal boundary — while remaining transparent elsewhere would be catastrophic precisely because standard evaluation would miss it, since most evaluation prompts are not near that boundary. A concrete operationalization of the threshold: if you measure interpreter accuracy as a function of prompt distance from the reward decision boundary (the surface where the reward model transitions from positive to negative), a dangerous phase transition would appear as a discontinuous drop in interpreter accuracy concentrated within epsilon of that boundary while accuracy elsewhere remains high — this is a tractable experiment nobody has yet run systematically, though the tools (contrastive activation patching + reward model gradient estimation) exist. The deepest implication is that RLHF training duration and scale function as implicit adversarial training against any fixed interpreter, not through any agent-like planning but through the same blind selection pressure that produces antibiotic resistance — and like antibiotic resistance, the response cannot be "train the interpreter harder on the same data" but must involve either rotating interpreters faster than blindness can consolidate, or fundamentally changing what property the interpreter measures so that opacity in one representation cannot simultaneously blind it.
